en: Preface to the *Enlightening Resolve on the Diamond Sūtra*:
Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas, the true cause of Bodhisattvas, the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, and the fundamental basis of all living things.
Depending on whether one turns toward or away from it, there arises the distinction between the holy and the ordinary. Thus, we know that it is manifest in the daily activities of all beings.

All that was previously seen, heard, known, and perceived is the light of Prajñā; it depends entirely on whether one has faith or not. Therefore, it is said that the ocean of the Buddhas' wisdom is entered through faith.

Although those disciples who attained deliverance at the single assembly on Vulture Peak were freed from birth and death, they lacked the capacity for Buddhahood because they did not believe in this Dharma.
Thus, our World-Honored One labored to refine them through various means and rebuked them in manifold ways.

Yet those of inferior understanding repeatedly give rise to doubt, believing that this is not within the scope of their own wisdom. Because the root of doubt has not been uprooted, their fundamental wisdom does not manifest.

When they reach the assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata uses adamantine wisdom to decisively sever [their delusions], directly causing the emotions of both sages and ordinary beings to be exhausted and the views of arising and ceasing to perish. Thereupon, the light of originally existing wisdom is suddenly and fully revealed.
One begins to believe that one’s own mind is inherently pure, realizing that not a single dharma acts as an obstruction.

This *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* directly uproots the source of doubt and is taught for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle; it is by no means something that can be understood by those of shallow learning or meager virtue.
Therefore, Huangmei used this to seal his mind, because the non-establishment of even a single dharma constitutes the true eye of the Chan school. In the past...

Maitreya (Devaputra) enumerated twenty-seven doubts to explain this single sutra; yet, as these doubts remain latent beyond the literal words, those in this land who study the teachings cling to the vessel while losing the finger that points at the moon.
Those who have attained the meaning and forgotten the words since ancient times have been rare. Since my youth, I have been able to recite it, yet until now I have not understood it.
I often reflect on how the Great Master Huineng attained sudden realization of this mind under a single word—how could there not be awakening in every age?

Those who enter [this path] fail to open their true eye and, conversely, allow it to become an obstacle to their nature. While residing at Caoxi, I happened to expound upon this once for the great assembly;
suddenly, I attained awakening, and the doubts that lay beyond words were instantly clarified within my mind’s eye.
Truly, this Dharma is free from the marks of letters and cannot be understood through thought, deliberation, or discrimination. Therefore, I have presented a mere glimpse of it here.
This was first carved in Lingnan as a gift of Dharma; it was carved again at Wuyun and once more at Nanyue. My disciple Fang Yu, having seen it, received it with faith.
Now it is being carved again at Wumen so that the fourfold assembly may widely fulfill their vows and together open the adamantine eye of true insight.
To have faith in one's own mind is the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood; let this serve as the vanguard of such realization.
Composed by the Daoist Qing of Mount Han on the first day of the long winter month in the Bingchen year.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty: *The Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Composed by the Chan monk Hanshan Shi Deqing of Caoxi.

Regarding the two characters "Vajra" (Jingang) in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, commentators generally take their meaning to be "firm and sharp, capable of cutting. This is a general explanation. However...
It is true that there is indeed a "vajra-jewel" in the Western Regions; this jewel is most hard and indestructible, yet it can destroy all other objects.
To take this jewel as a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom), which can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), may seem plausible at first glance, but in general, it does not accord with the Buddha’s intent;
it is merely the product of ordinary, habitual views and knowledge.
"Prajñā" is here translated as "wisdom," which is the very heart of the Buddha; it refers to what is called the Buddha's wisdom.
"Pāramitā" means "reaching the other shore," indicating the ultimate limit of this mind.
The title of this work, *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, specifically highlights the Buddha’s singular diamond-like mind as expounded in this sutra.
Listen. Furthermore, the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) is the fundamental mind by which a Buddha cultivates the causes and realizes the fruit.

Now, appearing in the world to teach and transform sentient beings, he employs this mind entirely. Teaching the bodhisattvas now to take the adamantine mind as the fundamental cause for cultivation is because it serves as the initial gateway for entering the Mahāyāna; therefore, he specifically reveals it to sever their doubts. This is because this mind is not...
Because the common sentiments of worldly beings are such, the entire world is unable to know the Buddha. Furthermore, the Buddha was originally not a person of this world;
that he has now come from nowhere into the human realm causes everyone who sees him to give rise to doubt.
In his daily conduct and activities, every single detail was unlike that of others. His speech was different; his rules and regulations were different.
In every matter and every practice, he acted in opposition to the world. Consequently, his movements aroused suspicion.
It is no wonder that the various devas and māras all desired to harm him, and that Devadatta and Ajātaśatru both sought to kill him, while all people alike gave rise to slander.
Therefore it is said: "When I appear in the world, all devas, humans, asuras, non-Buddhists, and māras shall be struck with alarm and doubt.

This is precisely it. Not only do devas and humans harbor doubts, but even among my disciples, the foremost ones such as Kāśyapa and others, all harbor doubts regarding the Buddha, because the Dharma I preach is at times empty and at times existent, and at times right and at times wrong; or—
Whether praising or censuring, encouraging or rebuking, his words were entirely inconsistent.
Consequently, all the disciples who heard him were filled with doubt and did not believe him, saying, "Could it be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha to disturb and confuse our minds?
If even the foremost disciples reacted in this way, the state of those newly trained can be easily imagined; for the Dharma taught by the Buddha is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
"However, it has already been thirty years since the Buddha appeared in the world and delivered this one discourse on the Dharma.
Yet my disciples still harbor doubts and do not believe; thus, the Buddha’s grievance has indeed been long-standing.

Today, fortunately, Śūnyatā-janman (Subhūti) possesses some insight and has caught a glimpse of a portion of the World-Honored One’s majesty, whereupon he suddenly gave rise to praise. Therefore, the World-Honored One..."

Because of their doubts, he resolved and shattered them. He then revealed his own single, adamantine true mind, declaring it and presenting it to them, so that they might attain awakening and be free from doubt. This caused all who heard it to have their manifold doubts suddenly severed.
Therefore, this sutra is the Buddha’s manifestation of his own mind to sever the doubts of his disciples who study the Buddha-way; it is not [merely] speaking...

Prajñā can sever the afflictions of sentient beings. If it were otherwise, one would simply observe that every instance in the sūtra concerns the doubts of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, or the doubts regarding the Buddha’s mind; the Buddha manifested this mind precisely to shatter those doubts.
When has he ever said that wisdom severs the afflictions of sentient beings? Therefore, the title of this sūtra refers solely to the Dharma, not [to the person].
This is by way of analogy. It merely cuts away the doubts of disciples; it proceeds to cut away the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.
This sutra has a single flavor, taking the severing of doubt and the generation of faith as its primary purpose.

For those who study the Way, faith is the foundation and doubt acts as an obstacle. Thus, there are three kinds of doubt: doubt regarding the person, doubt regarding the Dharma, and doubt regarding oneself. Doubt regarding the person refers to identifying...

People are not sincere. For instance, when disciples hear the Buddha speak of the *rūpakāya* (form body) and the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), or the great body and the small body, they do not know which one is the true Buddha; this is a person in doubt. Furthermore, regarding his preaching of the Dharma:
he has just said it exists, yet he again says it is empty; he has just said it is empty, yet he again says it is not empty. Because his words are inconsistent, [this teaching] is most... [difficult].
This is doubtful; this is doubt regarding the Dharma. There may be those who, upon hearing it, are able to believe and do not doubt the Dharma;
yet, seeing that the Dharma is vast, they doubt their own faculties are small, believing they are incapable of receiving and upholding it, or unable to practice it—this is doubt regarding oneself.
Now, within this sutra, all three types of doubt are present. The Buddha, following the points of doubt raised by Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kongsheng), immediately addresses them one by one.

[This] refutes [the opposing views] and suddenly severs that doubt; that is to say, "doubt and regret are forever exhausted, and one dwells securely within true wisdom"—this is the purport of this sutra.

Regarding this sutra, those who have attempted to explain it in this region are extremely numerous, yet none accord with the Buddha’s intention. Only the Venerable Vasubandhu of the Western Regions...

[Sa]. It is most appropriate to divide the sutra into twenty-seven sections of doubt. However, although the intent originated with the Sage, the treatise has already been transmitted and translated here in this land.
Furthermore, translators differ in their skill and artistry; when words fail to convey the meaning, they instead create obstructions, making it difficult for students to comprehend.
This subtle and profound purport cannot be fully expressed by speech; once it falls [into words]...
Words that attempt to explain it immediately become dross; how much more so when one clings to coarse and superficial characters—how could such things reach the Sublime?
This commentary’s difficulty in describing the Buddha-mind is not without the ugliness of a mere imitation of another's frown. It is just as when worldly people compose biographies:
they can only recount events, but cannot transmit the spirit. This is the difficulty. Therefore, this present work resolves doubts and elucidates the Sublime.
In this case, the doubt arising from the initial mention of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) takes precedence as the primary concern.

If that state of doubt is fully revealed, then the Buddha’s discourse on dispelling that doubt will become self-evident without requiring further explanation. Therefore, this commentary first presents the doubt prior to the main text.
He broke it down by following the traces section by section; forgetting words, he attained realization and grasped the essence for himself.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
[This is] explained. These are the protocols for the Buddha’s dwelling in the world and his preaching of the Dharma; all have been fully explicated elsewhere, so I shall not elaborate further here.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location. When he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and spread out a seat.
And sat. [The Master] explained:
"This is the Buddha’s ordinary way of living while remaining in the world. His daily conduct and every movement of his countenance were no different from those of the common people;
there was nothing extraordinary about them. It was only that within, there was a single point that differed from others. Those who know this are rare."

At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare it is, World-Honored One!"
[The Master] explained: "The Tathāgata dwells in the world with a daily life as ordinary as that of any other person.
As for that single point of difference within, no one has known it face-to-face until today, when he was suddenly scrutinized by Subhūti;
thus he sighed, 'How rare! Alas! The Tathāgata and his disciples have been together for thirty years, yet all along [the truth] remained unknown."
Regarding the places where the Buddha walked and dwelt, they did not know them and thus let them pass as ordinary matters, claiming he was just like everyone else.

Consequently, whenever the Buddha spoke, they mostly harbored doubts and did not believe him. Had it not been for Subhūti seeing through this, would there ever have been anyone who truly knew the Buddha?
"The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
This explains that Subhūti’s praise of the Buddha’s rare and marvelous qualities is precisely his direct witness to this single piece of the Tathāgata’s bitter heart.
A bodhisattva is a disciple who learns from the Buddha; that is, one who was formerly within the Small Vehicle and has now first resolved upon the Great [Vehicle].
Those who "ride upon the mind" are the Bodhisattvas of Empty and Disturbed Minds. The Buddha single-mindedly protects and remembers these people;
he has no other intention than merely wishing to entrust them with this mind. As for "protecting and remembering," it is because of the Buddha’s original vow in appearing in the world:
he desires only that all sentient beings be no different from the Buddha, so that every person may attain Buddhahood, thereby fulfilling this [vow].
[The Buddha’s] mind [is thus]. However, sentient beings have meager merit and heavy defilements; their resolve is timid and weak, and they are unable to bear the burden, being like infants.
The Buddha is like a compassionate mother who protects and attends to an infant, never letting go for even a single moment.

He provides every kind of thorough care, protection, and affectionate concern, just as one would protect a young child. This so-called "protective mindfulness" (nirantarānusmṛti) is solely intended for all [sentient beings].
Sentient beings continue until they finally attain Buddhahood; therefore, it is called "entrustment" (*parindanā*).
Yet, [the Buddha] did not speak of this explicitly, but rather employed subtle and secret skillful means (*upāya*) to guide them accordingly; hence, it is called "skillful. As the Sūtra says:
"By means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, I guide sentient beings, desiring that all sentient beings may reach the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."
This is called the entrustment of protective mindfulness.
World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?
Explanation: This passage describes how Śūnyatāputra specifically inquired about the method for settling the mind (*anxin*).
Previously, when he was practicing the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), he was solely intent on saving himself and unwilling to save other beings; thus, his mind was small.

Now, having been refined by the Tathāgata through various means for over twenty years, he has been stirred to arouse the resolve to save all beings. Therefore, he is called a "Great-Minded Being" and is designated as a Bodhisattva. It is essential [to understand this].
He causes those below to transform sentient beings and intends to seek the fruit of Buddhahood above.
Because these individuals are willing to benefit living beings on their own accord, it is called "arousing the bodhicitta. This Śāriputra has already gained faith in the Buddha-mind;

however, seeing only a Bodhisattva who has newly aroused the great mind, he has not yet realized the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*bhūtatathatā-śūnyatā*). This is difficult to distinguish from the partial emptiness previously grasped. For this reason—
The nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna can be grasped and clung to as a basis for settling the mind.

Now, having abandoned the former emptiness yet not having attained true emptiness—meaning that one has neither gained new realization in advancing nor lost one's former ground—this is called "the distracted mind by emptiness.

Because one is single-mindedly attached to verbal designations, the latencies (*vāsanā*) have not been forgotten; thus, there must still be dwelling and clinging, as well as attachment to a fixed certainty.
The fruit of Buddhahood can be sought; one might think that reaching the fruit of Buddhahood is one's dwelling place.
Yet, one must first seek the fruit of Buddhahood above and necessarily desire to transform sentient beings below. Only when all sentient beings have been delivered does one attain Buddhahood.
Now, with our own eyes we see the sentient beings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, immeasurable and boundless; when will they ever be delivered?
[The afflictions] may be exhausted, yet sentient beings are not exhausted; how, then, can one attain the fruit of Buddhahood?

Because the mind that seeks [this goal] is urgent, this mind is restless and cannot be subdued. Therefore, Subhūti specifically requested the method for dwelling the mind securely and subduing the mind.
Nevertheless, Subhūti had already perceived the Buddha’s mind and marveled at its rarity.
Furthermore, why did he open his mouth to ask only these two questions? It was because everyone thought to themselves, "Today the World-Honored One has already attained the fruit of fruition.
Thus, seeing that the World-Honored One was so at ease and composed in his daily activities, they wondered:
"How should those who have only now first resolved to seek the fruit of Buddhahood settle their minds, for their minds are not yet stable?"

"Abiding. How does one subdue it?"—this is the intent of the question. Regarding "settling the mind": it is like the Second Patriarch attending upon Bodhidharma and requesting the Dharma for settling the mind. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall settle it for you. The Patriarch said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is ultimately unobtainable. Bodhidharma said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. However, under the gate of the Patriarchs, everything is resolved in a single word. What is meant here? It refers to the state where there is no longer any grasping at the mind as something to be attained. This is called "settling the mind. As for "how to subdue it," this means that when one realizes that the mind is fundamentally unobtainable, there is nothing further to be subdued. If one still harbors thoughts of subduing, one has not yet truly settled the mind. Therefore, the Patriarch said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. This is what is meant by "abiding. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "how to subdue it," it means that once the mind is settled, there is no longer anything to be subdued. If one perceives the mind as having a form or substance, one will inevitably seek to subdue it; however, since the mind is originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is settled, there is nothing to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being unmoved within the midst of all phenomena. If one is moved by external conditions, one has not yet attained abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is unmoving; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is unmoving, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as having movement, one will seek to subdue it; however, since movement is originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is unmoving, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from both gain and loss, praise and blame, and all dualistic dharmas. If one is still affected by these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from gain and loss; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from gain and loss, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as being subject to gain and loss, one will seek to subdue it; however, since gain and loss are originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from gain and loss, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from birth and death, coming and going, and the cycle of samsara. If one is still bound by these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from birth and death; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from birth and death, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as being subject to birth and death, one will seek to subdue it; however, since birth and death are originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from birth and death, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from the four elements, the five aggregates, and the six sense bases. If one is still attached to these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from the four elements; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from the four elements, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as being composed of the four elements, one will seek to subdue it; however, since the four elements are originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from the four elements, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from the three poisons, the eight winds, and all afflictions. If one is still afflicted by these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from the three poisons; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from the three poisons, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as being subject to the three poisons, one will seek to subdue it; however, since the three poisons are originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from the three poisons, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from the ten directions, the three times, and all conditioned phenomena. If one is still bound by these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from the ten directions; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from the ten directions, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as being subject to the ten directions, one will seek to subdue it; however, since the ten directions are originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from the ten directions, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, as well as from nirvana. If one is still attached to these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from the Triple Gem; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from the Triple Gem, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as being subject to the Triple Gem, one will seek to subdue it; however, since the Triple Gem is originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from the Triple Gem, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from the self, persons, sentient beings, and life-essence, as well as from the views of permanence and annihilation. If one is still bound by these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from the four marks; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from the four marks, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as being subject to the four marks, one will seek to subdue it; however, since the four marks are originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from the four marks, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from the mind, consciousness, thought, and cognition, as well as from the realm of emptiness. If one is still attached to these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from mind; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "how to subdue it," it means that when the mind is free from mind, there is no longer any need for subduing. If one perceives the mind as having a nature of mind, one will seek to subdue it; however, since the nature of mind is originally non-existent, there is nothing to be subdued. Thus, it is said: "When the mind is free from mind, there is no longer anything to be subdued. This is the meaning. Furthermore, "abiding" refers to the state of being free from the dhyānas, samādhis, and various meditative concentrations, as well as from the realm of signlessness. If one is still attached to these, one has not yet attained true abiding. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is free from dhyāna; this is called abiding. This is the meaning of "abiding. As for "
This was taken as the fundamental principle. Now, the World-Honored One has expounded many methods for settling the mind, revealing his compassionate concern;
yet, the ultimate teaching is simply that when one seeks the mind, it is ultimately unattainable. Therefore, prior to the Fourth Patriarch, all used the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the mind;
from the Sixth Patriarch at Huangmei onwards, all have used the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to seal the mind. Thus...
This sutra does not consist of the characteristics of words and letters; it cannot be viewed through the lens of speech or script. It resides entirely in the subtlety that transcends words.
Throughout this sutra, whenever the phrase "What do you think? appears, it serves to counter-verify the listener's doubts.
Because the minds of the multitude give rise to doubt following the words, even before they are voiced, the mind has already stirred with thought; this is termed the "division of mental speech."
"It is distinct; it is precisely the habitual tendencies of names and concepts.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you, son of good family, daughter of good family."
A person who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and subdue their mind in this manner.
This explains Subhūti’s question, which implies that a bodhisattva who has resolved upon the path must not settle their mind in the same way as a Buddha does.
Zizai said, "I had thought that if one seeks to become a Buddha, one must necessarily act in the same manner as a Buddha's daily conduct;
only then would one be a Buddha. Yet I observe that the Buddha’s mind is so peaceful and at ease, whereas the Bodhisattva’s mind cannot abide in peace."
"How does one subdue [the mind] so that it becomes peaceful? The Buddha’s intended answer was: "A bodhisattva who seeks peace of mind need not seek it elsewhere;
simply by understanding my heart of protective mindfulness and entrustment as you have done, the mind will naturally become peaceful.
There is no need for any other form of subduing. Therefore, it is said: 'As you have said, one need only attain peace of mind.'"
"It is sufficient. What further subduing is there? It should simply be thus. Therefore it is said: 'Thus.
'So be it, World-Honored One; I wish and desire to hear.'"

[Subhūti] replied: "So be it. Śūnyatā-janman (Empty-Born) has directly believed in the Buddha’s mind without doubt. Since he has already seen the Buddha’s mind, there would seemingly be no need for further explanation;
yet, because the various bodhisattvas have not yet grasped its meaning, they desire to hear it again."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner.
This is the Buddha’s instruction on the method for settling the mind; the meaning will be explained in the following text. Previously, two matters were asked about: abiding and subduing.
Now, only subduing is permitted to be discussed, while abiding is not mentioned, because ordinary beings [possess] the two... [of views].
The vehicle. It is the persistent attachment to a dwelling place; this is what is called the habit-energy (*vāsanā*).
Now, those who aspire to enter the Mahāyāna must first eliminate this habit-energy, for both sentient beings and nirvāṇa are not real dharmas and are both unattainable.
It takes only names and words as its essence. Once names and words are relinquished, habitual tendencies are suddenly emptied. The mind does not require subduing;
it becomes naturally serene and enters into quiescent extinction. Therefore, the teaching merely instructs one to subdue the mind, without mentioning where it should abide.
I fear that this will lead to the reinforcement of habitual tendencies; that is to say, the wild mind does not cease. When it ceases, that is *bodhi*.
Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments, and there will be no separate "sacred" understanding. The Buddha does not bind people with real dharmas, and therefore he does not speak of "abiding."
All classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether possessing form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception.
"I cause all of them to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.
Although in this way I liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in reality there is no sentient being who attains liberation. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, he is not a bodhisattva."
[Commentary: This is the World-Honored One’s direct instruction on the method of contemplating the settling of the mind (*anxin*).

Now, for a Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind [on enlightenment], there are only two concerns: that which is sought, which is the fruit of Buddhahood; and that which is to be transformed, which are sentient beings.

The reason the mind is not yet settled is that one has not yet perceived sentient beings as they truly are (*yathābhūta*). Before one's eyes, there are only sentient beings; when will they ever all be delivered? Sentient beings...
If sentient beings are not fully liberated, the fruit of Buddhahood is difficult to seek; one’s perception of the path becomes increasingly long and distant.

Consequently, the mind becomes restless, leading to an unremitting state of urgency. Thus, one seeks to subdue this mind. Now, the Buddha teaches the method for liberating sentient beings by taking the contemplation of non-self as primary.
Furthermore, the multitude of sentient beings perceived by a Bodhisattva is so vast that they are difficult to liberate all at once.

Because one possesses the mark of self (*ātman*), one perceives the mark of persons (*pudgala*). When persons face one another, what limit is there to the sentient beings within the three thousandfold world-system?
Moreover, their births continue without end; one ought to fear that they can never be exhausted. Yet, one has not yet seen that the essence of sentient beings is fundamentally *tathatā* (suchness).
Although sentient beings are numerous, they are comprised in total of twelve categories; even if they were immeasurable, they would still be nothing more than this.
Twelfth: Examining each of the twelve categories individually, they are subsumed within the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation.
Within these four modes of birth, there are no more than the two dharmas of form and mind. Regarding form, there is nothing beyond the realms of form and formlessness;
regarding mind, there is likewise nothing beyond the realms of perception and non-perception. Even reaching the very pinnacle, one merely arrives at [the summit of existence].
Neither existent nor non-existent—these twelve categories exhaust the realm of sentient beings. What more could there be?

Furthermore, these twelve classes are called "sentient beings. The form and mind of sentient beings are fundamentally a provisional combination; since they are a provisional combination, [they lack inherent nature].
Thus, sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent. Sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent; they are perceived as existing only through deluded vision.

If one contemplates sentient beings as fundamentally non-existent, then sentient beings are inherently suchness (*tathatā*). Since sentient beings are suchness, they all constitute quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).
This means that all of them are brought into *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa*. What difficulty could there be in this? As Vimalakīrti said: "All sentient beings..."

Birth is ultimately quiescent; it does not undergo further cessation. In this manner, one brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, yet in reality, not a single sentient being has attained parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because from the very beginning there is no self.
Because there is a self, there is a person; because there is a person, there are sentient beings, life-spanners, and individuals.

To possess these four marks is not to be called a bodhisattva. How, then, can one speak of "delivering sentient beings"? Therefore, a bodhisattva delivering sentient beings should contemplate non-self.
Where there is no self, there is no person. Since there is neither self nor person, the realm of sentient beings is naturally quiescent.
Extinction. When sentient beings are in a state of quiescent extinction, the fruit of Buddhahood is not distant; why then fear its long duration?
For this reason, a bodhisattva should contemplate non-self. As the subsequent text states: "Knowing that all phenomena are without self, one attains the stage of patience (kṣānti)."
"This is truly a Bodhisattva. △ Question:
In the Buddha’s teaching, the Bodhisattva saves sentient beings, taking giving as the foundation. Those who receive what is given are all sentient beings.
Now, if all sentient beings are empty, then for the acts of giving one performs, who is there to receive? Therefore, below—
Mañjuśrī replied: "A bodhisattva’s practice of giving does not necessarily involve attachment to the mark of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving by dwelling in no phenomenon whatsoever. That is to say, one should not dwell on form when practicing giving;
one should not dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should [practice] like this..."
"This is giving that does not dwell upon signs.
This explains the doubt regarding the attachment to signs. Subhūti, having heard that all sentient beings are empty, then doubted, saying:
"If sentient beings are already empty, then when a Bodhisattva practices giving, there would be no recipient; for the six sense objects do not exist..."
Since birth is fundamentally empty, it is said that "one should have no abiding place. This teaching is intended to prevent attachment to the characteristics of sentient beings and their defilements.

Furthermore, to suppress potential doubts—asking, "If one does not abide in characteristics, how can there be merit?"—the text below answers that merit which is free from characteristics is even greater.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit and virtue cannot be measured or conceived.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the empty space in the eastern direction be measured or conceived? "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, [it is the same for the merit of such a bodhisattva].
"Can the empty space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, it is the same with the merit of a bodhisattva who practices giving without dwelling on signs; that merit, too, cannot be measured."
Explanation: This resolves the doubt regarding attachment to signs and demonstrates the sublime practice of signlessness.
However, when a Bodhisattva practices giving, it is primarily for the sake of seeking merit. If the mind seeking merit becomes attached to signs, then that merit will not be great.

Therefore, the World-Honored One provisionally pointed out that merit free from signs is even greater, so as to bring peace to the mind. Yet, giving while attached to signs remains confined within the realm of existence.
As for marks, the mark of sentient beings is but a single atom. Even if one were able to obtain merit from this, how great would that merit be?

Now, when one is correctly bestowing gifts upon sentient beings, if one does not perceive a giver, nor a receiver, nor the object being given—if these three wheels are all empty and there is no mark to dwell upon—then the merit of dwelling in non-attachment to marks is such that its merit [is immeasurable].
It is inconceivable; therefore, it is likened to empty space.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed. [Commentary:

This concludes the demonstration of the method for settling the mind (*śamatha*). Since the previous question concerned the inability of the mind to abide peacefully, it was necessary to bring it down [into stability].
I prostrate. Regarding the World-Honored One’s teaching on the method for subduing [the mind], it simply takes the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) as primary.
When there is no self, there is no person. When both person and self are forgotten, one's own mind becomes quiescent. When one's own mind is quiescent, all sentient beings are likewise quiescent.
Since sentient beings are already quiescent, there is no need to seek a Buddha. This [seeking] is merely a state of frantic pursuit.
The mind comes to rest. When the sentiments of grasping and rejecting are forgotten, both internal and external are empty, and the single mind remains unmoving;
this is what is called the method for settling the mind. Therefore, it concludes with the word "Thus."
△ Doubt: Previously, one performed merit through giving to transform sentient beings below, solely for the purpose of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above.
Now, since the marks of sentient beings are empty and the three wheels are essentially quiescent, the cause would be rendered a mere fiction.
How can a cause devoid of marks be used to seek a fruit possessed of marks? Moreover, we currently see that the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are perfectly manifest.
It is not that a cause characterized by signlessness can be apprehended; this is because one perceives the Tathāgata through signs.
Therefore, the Buddha refutes this, saying: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the marks of his body? No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the marks of his body. Why is this? The marks of the body spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not marks of the body."
[The Buddha] said: "Subhūti, whatever has marks is entirely empty and false. If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata."
[Śāriputra] said, "I understand. This directly points to the wondrous practice of signlessness (*animitta*).

Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) had heard of the cause that is signless, yet he consequently doubted this cause, being unable to seek the Buddha-fruit which possesses signs; thus, he perceived the Tathāgata through signs.

This was because he was attached to the signs of the Buddha’s emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and had not yet seen the true essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The World-Honored One questioned and refuted his perception of signs. Śūnyatā-utpanna—
He immediately grasped the essential meaning. Therefore, the Buddha directly stated that one cannot see the Tathāgata through marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
This is because the body spoken of by the Tathāgata is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); thus, it is called "no-body. Yet, even the Dharma-body is not characterized by marks;
it is upon the very marks of all phenomena that one perceives their lack of marks—that is how one sees the Tathāgata. It is not that there is no Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Apart from all phenomena, there is no separate characteristic or form; this is clearly the cause of signlessness that accords with the fruit of signlessness.
A doubt arises: If one accords with the fruit of signlessness by means of the cause of signlessness, this principle is extremely profound and difficult [to fathom].
It was difficult to believe and thus gave rise to doubt.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases as these..."

"Will they give rise to true faith? The Buddha told Subhūti, "Do not speak thus. After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit who are able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as the truth.
You should know that such persons have planted roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but have already [planted them] under countless..."

Subhūti, those who have served as many as ten million Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and upon hearing these phrases, give rise to even a single thought of pure faith—they are all known and seen by the Tathāgata. Such sentient beings shall obtain immeasurable merit. Why is this?
Because these sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span.

There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas. Why is this? If these sentient beings take up marks with their minds, they are then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If they take up the mark of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Why is this? If one grasps at the marks of what is not the Dharma, one is immediately attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
For this reason, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one grasp at what is not the Dharma. By this principle, the Tathāgata has always said to you bhikṣus:
"Know that my teaching of the Dharma is like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so what is not the Dharma."
[Commentary: This directly reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Because of the preceding emptiness, there arose the initial attachment to the cause of having marks (*nimitta*).

The Buddha refuted this by means of giving without dwelling on marks. Subsequently, there arose doubt regarding the cause of marklessness, such that one could not accord with the fruit of having marks;
this was because one clung to the Buddha as having a specific appearance. The Buddha refuted this by means of the Dharma-body being without marks. This is...
It is clear that by means of a cause without marks, one accords with a fruit without marks. If this is so, then both cause and effect are empty, and both person and phenomena are extinguished.
This principle is extremely profound, difficult to believe and difficult to understand; therefore, he questioned the Buddha: "I do not know if there might be someone who can believe in this Dharma?
"Perhaps" (*po*) is used here as a concessive particle meaning "it may be so. The phrase "words and chapters" refers back to the aforementioned absence [of marks].
Regarding the doctrine of the causes and effects of marks, the Buddha replied: "Is it not the case that there are such people?
However, those who believe in this Dharma are not ordinary persons; rather, it is only those who maintain the precepts and cultivate merit who are able to believe.
Furthermore, such a person has not planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; they have done so under immeasurable tens of thousands of millions."
Those who plant roots of goodness before the Buddha are those who have long planted deep roots; only then can they believe.
For such beings of great capacity, even a single thought of faith—I fully know and see that the merit they obtain is already immeasurable.
It is clear that this merit of signlessness surpasses the merit sought through signs. Why is this so?
Regarding "signlessness": can one obtain great merit thereby? It is because these sentient beings no longer possess the signs of self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
Not only do they lack these four signs, but all signs of existence and non-existence are entirely empty.
Therefore, it is said that there is no sign of dharmas, nor any sign of non-dharmas. For these sentient beings, the mind does not grasp.

Because they are characterized by signs, all things are devoid of them. If one were to grasp at the signs of either dharma or non-dharma for even a single thought-moment, one would immediately be attached to the four marks.
Because one does not grasp at signs, both mind and objects are empty; such is the excellence of the merit obtained. This is the power of the Tathāgata’s true knowledge and vision;
therefore, I instruct bodhisattvas that they should not grasp at the signs of either dharma or non-dharma. Why?

For this reason, once one enters this Dharma, both person and dharma are empty. To suddenly abandon all grasping and yet give rise to the various realms of existence—how could this be a trivial matter?
Therefore, I have always instructed my disciples that they must relinquish even the Dharma. However, to relinquish the Dharma is to relinquish emotional attachment;
when attachment is forgotten, wisdom becomes perfect. Thus it is said: "Even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so that which is not the Dharma."
△ Doubt. Because Subhūti heard the Buddha say that the Buddha is not a form-characteristic and that the Dharma cannot be grasped, he gave rise to this doubt:

"If both the Buddha and the Dharma are without characteristics, then there would be neither Buddha nor Dharma. Yet, how can we deny what is currently seen—the Buddha attaining bodhi and presently preaching the Dharma?
Why do you say they do not exist? This is a doubt regarding the contradiction between the Buddha’s own words.
Therefore, it is refuted below.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

“Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma called ‘anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,’ nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could preach.
Why is this? All dharmas preached by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and inexpressible; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.”
"Dharma. Why is this? All worthy sages and saints are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
This explains that both "Buddha" and "Dharma" are simultaneously dispelled.

As soon as the thought of there being a Buddha or a Dharma sprouts within Subhūti’s mind—what is called the conceptualization of mental speech—the Buddha anticipates this and shatters it; therefore, he calls out [to him].
He then questioned him, saying: "What do you think? How does your mind differentiate?
Furthermore, is there anything to be attained in the Buddha’s bodhi? Or is there any dharma taught by the Tathāgata? He questioned him thus in order to examine his understanding.
Subhūti, having grasped the intent, set forth his realization, stating that he understood what the Buddha had said. Originally...
There is no fixed dharma; this is itself bodhi. Furthermore, there is no fixed dhaṛma that the Tathāgata could speak of.

This emptiness gives rise to a profound realization of the Tathāgata’s principle of non-appropriation. It is not only the Tathāgata, but all worthies and sages as well, who possess distinctions based on unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);
therefore, these are not to be appropriated. This concludes the intent of opening up the provisional to reveal the real.
A single glimpse has been revealed.

△ [Doubt. Subhūti has already grasped the principle that there is neither Buddha nor Dharma; however, he does not yet know how one who accords with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) can obtain such preeminent merit.
Therefore, the Tathāgata below refutes this by means of the departure from marks (lakṣaṇa).

“Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, “It would be very great, World-Honored One.”
Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is someone who, from this sutra, receives, upholds, and even explains as little as a four-line verse to others, their merit shall surpass the former.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because all Buddhas and the unsurpassed... [of all Buddhas]... [arise from this].
The Dharma of *samyaksambodhi* all issues forth from this sutra. Subhūti, that which is called the Buddha-Dharma is, in fact, not the Buddha-Dharma.
Explanation: This demonstrates that merit characterized by signlessness is the most supreme because it reveals the Dharma characterized by signlessness.
Although Subhūti has already realized the principle of signlessness, he merely did not yet know how to accord with the principle of signlessness to attain merit characterized by signlessness.
How can this merit surpass that which possesses signs? Therefore, the Buddha first used meritorious giving with signs as a standard for comparison;
yet the merit of upholding even a four-line verse is far more sublime. This is because all Buddhas are born from this Prajñāpāramitā;
thus it is said, "Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas. For this reason, [the former] is [inferior].
"Great! It is as the worldly saying goes: 'A mother is noble because of her son.

Thus, while Prajñāpāramitā is that which gives birth to the Buddhas and the Dharma, Prajñā itself is fundamentally not the Buddhas or the Dharma. Therefore it is said: 'That which is called the Buddhas and the Dharma...'"
This is precisely not the Buddha-dharma.
△ [The interlocutor] raises a doubt, saying: "If the Dharma is such that nothing can be spoken and the Buddha is such that nothing can be accomplished, then both are unattainable.
Yet, in the past, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma of the Four Truths for us Śrāvakas; this is indeed the Dharma. We rely upon it..."
To cultivate this is to attain the fruit. We abide in reliance upon nirvāṇa; this is that which has an abode.
How is it, World-Honored One, that all these are non-existent? This is the conceptualization and verbal expression of this great assembly.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first raised the matter of the minor fruits and questioned Subhūti, thereby refuting them on their behalf.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A stream-enterer is called one who has 'entered the flow,' yet there is nothing entered.
He does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; therefore, he is called a stream-enterer. Subhūti, at [this]—
"What do you think? Does a Sakṛdāgāmin have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A Sakṛdāgāmin is so called because he returns once more; yet in reality, there is no coming or going."
"This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think? Can an Anāgāmin have the thought:
'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin'? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because an Anāgāmin..."
He is called "one who does not come back" (Anāgāmin), yet in reality there is no such thing as "not coming back. For this reason, he is named Anāgāmin.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have the thought, "I have attained the path of an Arhat"? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because, in truth, there is no dharma that can be called 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have the thought, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat,' he would immediately be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
World-Honored One, the Buddha has said that I am foremost among men in attaining the Samādhi of Non-contention; I am the foremost in being free from desire."
"Arhat. World-Honored One, I do not harbor this thought: 'I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
This is because, Subhūti, in reality there is nothing practiced; yet Subhūti is named 'one who delights in araṇā.'"
The practice of Araṇa.

This clearly demonstrates the True Teaching of non-abiding. Because the great assembly has heard that the Buddha is not to be sought and that the Dharma is not to be grasped, they would consequently advance toward attainment with nothing in which to abide.
Yet, how can this be, when the World-Honored One formerly taught me the voice-hearer [vehicle]?
[They] hear [the teaching] so as to leave birth-and-death behind and dwell securely in nirvana; it is not that there is no dharma or no fruit in which one may dwell.

Yet why does the World-Honored One now say that all Buddha-dharmas are non-existent? This is because those of the Hīnayāna have not yet forgotten the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for names and words, and they cling to the existence of real dharmas.
Thus, they find it difficult to enter Prajñāpāramitā and frequently give rise to doubt. The World-Honored One, therefore, provisionally uses the awakening born of emptiness to...
This is a comprehensive explanation. Therefore, he cites a past result as a retroactive proof, asking: "What do you think? This means: "How is it in your mind?
The Sanskrit term *srotāpanna* is translated here as "entering the stream. "Entering" (*ru*) means "to go against" (*ni*). It refers to going against the flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
However, the expression "going against the flow" is used merely in the sense of not entering the six sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); it is not [an actual physical reversal].
There is that which can be reversed; there is that into which one may enter and abide.

The *Sakṛdāgāmin*—here translated as "One Who Comes Back Once"—is so called because they have a single remaining grade of afflictions (*kleśa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). They need only return once more to the desire realm to sever them, after which they shall proceed forever beyond.
This, too, does not involve actual coming and going or a real place of abiding. The *Anāgāmin*—this...
"Non-coming" means that one will never again come to take birth in the desire realm; it is simply this.
Nor is there any place of non-coming where one might dwell. "Arhat," which here means "non-birth," refers to seeing that all those phenomena are entirely non-existent;
since in reality no phenomena exist, the single mind does not arise. It is simply this. Furthermore, one has never engaged in [conceptualization].
He thought: "I am an Arhat. Yet there is no state of an Arhat that can be dwelled upon.
If an Arhat himself were to think, "I am an Arhat," and become attached to this recognition, he would be no different from the cognitive views of ordinary sentient beings;
he would be clinging to the four marks. Subhūti tested this within himself and realized it was so, just as the World-Honored One has repeatedly stated:
"I have attained the *araṇā-samādhi*. Furthermore, you have praised me as the most supreme among men, and declared me to be the foremost *arhat* free from desire.

Having been thus extolled by the World-Honored One with such fervent words, I reflected within my own mind and found that not for a single thought-moment had I given rise to a mind of attachment, thinking, 'I am an *arhat* free from desire.'"
"Indeed, Han. If I had harbored such a thought, the World-Honored One would not have declared me a practitioner of tranquil seclusion.
As I observe it, from the very beginning, Nirvana has had no place of abiding; one can thus know that for the Tathāgata’s Bodhi, there is necessarily no principle of abiding.
What cause for doubt remains? This resolves the doubt regarding whether the Buddha-fruit has a place of abiding. [End of section]
This resolves the doubt that the Buddha must necessarily have attained realization.
△ The doubt says: Having heard the above instruction, it is clear that the fruit of Buddhahood is non-abiding.

Since the fruit has nothing to be accomplished, how can one account for the fact that we currently see the Tathāgata receiving the prediction from Dīpaṃkara? This would mean that the Buddha must necessarily have attained realization. Since there is [this appearance]...
As for the Buddha who has attained [enlightenment], could there not be a fruit in which he might abide? [Subhūti] answers below that there is nothing to be obtained.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he obtain anything in the Dharma?
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he truly obtained nothing in the Dharma."

[Subhūti] explains: This demonstrates the principle that, in the ultimate sense, there is nothing to be attained. Having heard the discourse on non-abiding, he has already realized that bodhi is non-abiding;
yet he then suspects that although bodhi is non-abiding, the fruit of Buddhahood must necessarily be something accomplished.

He wonders, "If there were no accomplishment of Buddhahood, how could it be transmitted? Therefore, the World-Honored One poses a counter-question to Subhūti to resolve this doubt, using the analogy of burning...
Although Dīpaṃkara Buddha spoke of bestowing a prediction of enlightenment, he merely sealed this mind; in truth, there was nothing to be attained.
Had there been anything to be attained, Dīpaṃkara would certainly not have bestowed the prediction upon me.
△ Doubt: Awakening is non-abiding and the fruit of Buddhahood is non-attainment. If this is so, then it would be unnecessary to adorn the Buddha-fields.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One instruct me to practice the bodhisattva path and adorn the Buddha-fields?
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely named 'adorning.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling upon form."
"When the mind arises based on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas, one should let the mind arise without abiding anywhere.
This is a direct instruction on the method for settling the mind (*śamatha*). Subhūti, harboring a doubt, says:
"If the Buddha has no attainment and there is no abiding in nirvāṇa, then why is it necessary to adorn the Buddha-lands? Those who cling to this doubt say that [one must] deliver...
The practice of one who has been born [into the path] truly requires the adornment of Buddha-fields, just as one might repair a temple;
this is the delusion of grasping at signs. Therefore, the World-Honored One questioned Subhūti: "Does a bodhisattva indeed adorn Buddha-fields?
Subhūti, having received the intent, replied: "It is not an adornment; it is called 'adornment'. How is this clarified? For the Buddha...
"Earth" refers to the Pure Land. Moreover, how could this Pure Land be adorned by the piling up of the seven treasures?
That which is seen by sentient beings as an impure land is, in fact, adorned by evil karma and consists of various instruments of suffering.
In the pure lands where the Buddhas dwell, one simply uses the pure mind of awakening to purify all defilements.
Once defiled karma is emptied, the land becomes naturally pure. Thus, the pure mind itself serves as the adornment; yet this adornment—
It is not the same as that. Therefore it is said: "It is not adornment; it is called adornment. Viewed in this light, a Bodhisattva’s adornment of Buddha-lands does not depend on anything external;
it is simply the purification of one's own mind. When the mind is pure, the land is naturally pure.
Thus it is said: "One should merely give rise to such a pure mind; there is no need to seek adornment elsewhere."
This is solemnity. Again, [Subhūti] doubts: "If it is said to be pure, how can the mind arise? The Buddha says: "How can the mind arise from purity?
It is simply that one should not give rise to a mind defiled by the six sense-objects; it is not that there is some purity to dwell upon while the mind arises.
What is meant is that when grasping falls away and emotions are forgotten, the pure mind manifests of itself. Therefore it is said: "One should abide nowhere..."
