Suppose there were a heap of the seven precious treasures, and someone were to take it and give it as a gift.

If another person were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the former merit would not equal one-hundredth part of the latter;
nor one-hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.
[Commentary: This praises the supreme merit of Prajñāpāramitā’s transcendence of marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

Now, if one practices wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) and yet does not attain *bodhi*, then those wholesome dharmas are not preeminent. Furthermore, by what dharma is anything considered preeminent?
The Buddha said that those who have realized *prajñā* are the most preeminent. Within a trichiliocosm, there are ten billion Mount Sumerus.

To fill this [space] with the seven treasures and the like may be called abundant; yet the merit of such giving does not equal the merit of attaining even a single four-line verse of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Because that [giving] involves grasping at signs and a craving for benefit, whereas the Prajñāpāramitā is free from signs, it is infinitely superior and beyond the reach of analogy.
△ Doubt: Subhūti, having heard the previous teaching that sentient beings and Buddhas are equal, thinks: "If they are indeed equal, then there are no sentient beings.

Why then does the Tathāgata say he shall deliver sentient beings? This implies the existence of the marks of self and person. The following section refutes this by means of the mutual forgetting of both person and self.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a self, he does not speak of a self; yet ordinary people imagine that there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) by the Tathāgata are, in truth, not ordinary beings; they are merely designated as "ordinary beings.
This explains that it refutes the doubt that the Buddha possesses a self or a personhood, thereby revealing the true self of the Dharmakāya.
What is called the equality of birth and Buddhahood means that in this equality there is neither Buddha nor sentient being. How, then, can one say, "I shall deliver sentient beings"?
"Sentient beings" refers to people. If I were to save sentient beings, then there would be a self. When "people" and "self" remain distinct, the four marks [of existence] are not extinguished.
This is what the orthodox school of the Gate calls "reaching the stage of the Dharma-body," yet it has not yet penetrated the phrase beyond the Dharma-body.
Therefore, the World-Honored One dispelled this with words, saying: "Do not say that the Tathāgata has a saving of sentient beings."
The thought "I have this thought" is precisely that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Yet, as the Tathāgata has said, even an ordinary person is not ultimately an ordinary person;
how could the Tathāgata still harbor the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*)? Thus, both the holy and the ordinary are extinguished, and the single path is level and uniform.
Herein, the profound purport of Prajñā reaches its ultimate limit.
△ Doubt: Since the Dharma-body is not a self, and the Reward-body cannot be seen through its marks, are these present thirty-two marks not, then, the Buddha?
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is.

The Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage king would also be a Tathāgata. Subhūti addressed [the Buddha]:
The Buddha said, “World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: “If one sees me by form, Or seeks me by sound, Such a person follows a deviant path And cannot see the Tathāgata.”
[Subhūti] explained: "This demonstrates that the manifested transformation body is not the true [Buddha], thereby revealing that the Dharma-body is free from all marks.

Having already realized that the Dharma-body is without self and that the Reward-body is without marks—and thus constitutes the True Buddha—Subhūti then doubted, wondering which Buddha it was that he currently saw endowed with the thirty-two marks.
This was a manifestation of the view that there exists a Buddha. The World-Honored One questioned him, saying: "If one can [perceive] by means of the thirty..."
Regarding the second point, "seeing the Tathāgata through marks": Subhūti held that the thirty-two marks necessarily constituted a Buddha.
The World-Honored One refuted this by citing the case of the Cakravartin King, thereby leading him to realize that one cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
The World-Honored One demonstrated this with a verse on the transcendence of marks, saying: "If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound..."
"I. This person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. △ [This is] Doubt.

When Subhūti heard the teaching that the retribution for dharmas is signless (*animitta*) and that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not real, he gave rise to the view that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is subject to annihilation.
Because he did not realize the true self of the Dharma-body, the Buddha refuted this by means of the principle of non-annihilation.
Subhūti, if you should have this thought: "The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection," Subhūti, do not have such a thought.
The Tathāgata has not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection. Subhūti, if you should have this thought: "Having set forth..."
Regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, do not think that it teaches the annihilation or cessation of all phenomena. Why is this?
One who has resolved upon the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them...

[The Buddha said: "Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is another person who, knowing that all phenomena are without self, attains patience (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that bodhisattvas do not accept merit? Subhūti...
"Subhūti, the merit produced by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with greed; therefore, it is said that 'merit is not received.

Explanation: This refutes the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). When Śūnyatā-sambhava heard it was taught that one should see the Buddha through the departure from signs, he consequently gave rise to the view of nihilism, claiming that the Tathāgata does not attain *bodhi* by means of the marks of perfection. The Buddha instructed him, saying:
Do not conceive such a thought. If one were to conceive such a thought, it would be to say that all dharmas are annihilated.
However, those who have resolved upon bodhicitta do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding dharmas; they merely speak of knowing that all dharmas are without self.

Furthermore, if there is a person who knows that all dharmas are without self and attains the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva surpasses the merit of one who gives away the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, because they do not accept merit.
What is meant by "not accepting" is not that it is utterly non-existent; rather, it means simply not being greedily attached to merit. This is what is called "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
There is no creator and no recipient; yet the karmic fruits of good and evil deeds are never forgotten.
Since the World-Honored One appeared in the world, he preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, yet spoke only of the single word "Non-existence" (wu).

Because the sentient beings of the nine realms universally cling to the notion that all phenomena possess a self, the Tathāgata used only this word "Non-existence" to shatter it. This is the Adamantine True Eye, which directly observes toward [the source].
This is the ultimate path. Therefore, the Gate of the Patriarchs’ single transmission and direct pointing enters only from here.
△ Doubt: Since it is said that there is no self and no one who receives blessings, yet we presently see the Tathāgata walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.

"Is this not the self of the Tathāgata? This is because the view that the three bodies are either identical or distinct has not been extinguished, and one has not yet realized the dharmakāya of equality.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, such a person..."
"Understand the meaning of what I have said. Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
[Subhūti] understood. This refers to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the Dharmakāya. Previously, Subhūti had taken the movement and stillness of physical demeanor to be...
"Tathāgata—this is merely a view of coming and going. How could a Tathāgata have coming or going? When one reaches this point, attachments fall away and emotions are forgotten;
movement and stillness are non-dual. Suchness and the limit of reality reach their ultimate subtlety here.

Yet, because the views of oneness and difference have not been discarded and the meaning of the three bodies as a single essence has not been realized, the following section uses the world of atoms to break through [these delusions]."
“Subhūti, if a good man or a good woman were to grind this great trichiliocosm into fine particles of dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of dust be very much? Subhūti replied, “It would be very much, World-Honored One.”
World-Honored One, why is this? If these multitudes of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called them "multitudes of atoms.
Why is that? What the Buddha calls "multitudes of atoms" is not actually a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as "multitudes of atoms.
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata calls the "trichiliocosm" is not actually a world; it is merely designated as a "world. Why is this? Why...
For this reason, Subhūti, if a world were truly existent, it would be a "single unified mass. The Tathāgata says that what is called a single unified mass is not actually a single unified mass;
it is merely designated as a "single unified mass. Subhūti, that which is a single unified mass is ineffable;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.

[The commentary] explains: This refutes the views of identity and difference. Because Śūnyatā-janman had not yet realized that the three bodies (trikāya) are one essence, the World-Honored One demonstrated this by means of the fact that the world of atoms is neither identical nor different. To speak of "atoms" implies they are not one;
that these are "worlds" implies they are not different. When atoms aggregate to form a world, they are different yet not different; when a world disperses to become [atoms], they are...
A minute particle (*paramāṇu*) is one yet not one. Viewed from this perspective, the characteristics of identity and difference (*ekatva-anyatva*) cannot be apprehended at all.
Because they cannot be apprehended, they do not exist as substantial realities. If the characteristics of identity and difference were real, they would constitute a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa*).
A unified whole is a view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); for that which is unified cannot be different, and that which is combined with difference...
Because they cannot be one. If atoms were substantially real, they could not aggregate to form a world;
if the world were substantially real, it could not disperse to become atoms. Fools take this to be a unified, composite phenomenon.
The Tathāgata says that a "unified whole" (ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa) is not so; it is called a unified whole precisely because it is free from the two extremes.
Since the two extremes are abandoned, it is inexpressible. However, ordinary beings are unable to distance themselves from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, or oneness and difference;
they are greedily attached to these matters and thus cannot realize the equality of the three bodies as one essence.
This is the principle of the body.
△ Doubt: Since the equal Dharma-body is such that all things are neither identical to it nor visible, why does the Buddha speak of four ways of seeing it?
Therefore, the following section refutes this objection.
Subhūti, if someone were to say, "The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span," what do you think, Subhūti?
Would that person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One. That person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.
Why is this? Because, World-Honored One, when the Buddha speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span..."
This "view" is not, in fact, a view of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span (intended to dispel these views in sentient beings).
It is merely called a view of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span (originally, the Buddha did not say that these four views exist).
Subhūti, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, act in this manner.

Knowing thus, seeing thus, and resolving with faith thus, one does not give rise to the notion of dharmas. Subhūti, that which is called the "notion of dharmas" has been taught by the Tathāgata as being no notion of dharmas;
it is merely designated as the "notion of dharmas."

[The Buddha] explained: This refutes the view that clings to the existence of a reality apart from characteristics. Subhūti had already realized the principle of the Dharmakāya, which is equal and suchness;

he consequently doubted the essence of the Dharmakāya, wondering: "Since the substance of the Dharmakāya cannot be perceived through characteristics, why did the World-Honored One speak of a view that is free from the four characteristics?
Fearing that Subhūti harbored this doubt within his mind, the Buddha questioned him, saying:
"Suppose someone were to say that the World-Honored One has taught the view of four characteristics. Do you think this person understands the meaning of what I have said?
Subhūti then realized the Buddha's intention and replied, "This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken.
Why is this? Because when the World-Honored One speaks of the view of four characteristics, it is not [the case that he intends them to be taken as such]."

In reality, there are characteristics and views that can be pointed out and described; [the teaching] is intended merely to dispel the clinging attachments of those who perceive such characteristics and views.
Therefore, it says "not. This word "not" differs from other instances of "not.

While the previous frequent uses of "not" all carried the sense of negation (it is not so), this present "not" is a term of total eradication, meaning to eliminate what is grasped within the minds of sentient beings.
This is merely the mutual perception of sentient beings; it is not that the Buddha taught such a mutual perception exists.

It is simply the mutual perception of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said: "This is called. These two characters, "this is called," are also different from what has been stated repeatedly; one should contemplate this deeply.
It is because all sentient beings are deluded within the realm of perceived forms (*nimitta*), and their attachments are so firm that they are difficult to shatter.

Therefore, the Buddha employs the diamond-like wisdom-mind (*vajra-citta-jñāna*) to pursue and destroy them, causing them to perceive the true essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of original wisdom.

Initially, they grasp at the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the body and mind, as well as the characteristics of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Thus, they practice giving while attached to these forms in order to seek Buddhahood.
Regarding merit, the World-Honored One refuted it by means of non-abiding. Next, [the disciple] clung to the mark of an existent bodhi; the Buddha refuted this by means of non-attainment.
Next, [the disciple] clung to the mark of the adornment of buddha-fields through giving; the Buddha refuted this by means of the fact that there are no fields to be adorned.
Next, [the disciple] clung to the mark of merit as something that evokes retribution; the Buddha refuted this by means of the fact that it is not a physical body of complete form.
Next, [the opponent] maintains that the Tathāgata definitely possesses the characteristics of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The Buddha refutes this by stating that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) are not real, and that the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) is free from characteristics.

Next, [the opponent] maintains that the *dharmakāya* definitely possesses the characteristic of a real self (*ātman*). The Buddha refutes this by stating that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*). Next, [the opponent] maintains that the Tathāgata...

The coming-to-be of the three bodies has three characteristics. The Buddha refutes them by showing they are neither identical nor different, refuting them layer after layer until all are found to be non-existent.
All characteristics vanish; the one mind has no place of reliance. When principle reaches its ultimate limit, emotion is forgotten. This directly points to the Dharmakāya, the true reality.
Since the delusive appearances that are perceived are empty, the delusive seeing that perceives them also subsides. This...
This is the ultimate pinnacle of true *prajñā*, the direct penetration of the *dharmakāya* along the upward path. Therefore, the Buddha cautioned:
"Those who give rise to the bodhicitta should know all phenomena thus, see them thus, and believe and understand them thus, without giving rise to the marks of phenomena.
Only upon reaching this state does one possess true knowledge, true vision, true faith, and true understanding.

Then one will forever not give rise to the perception and views of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This is the simultaneous forgetting of both person and phenomena; the simultaneous dissolution of both the sage and the ordinary person.

The path of words is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. To raise the mind is an error; to stir a thought is a deviation. Therefore, it is further sent forth [as a negation], saying:
"That which is called the characteristic of phenomena is also not the characteristic of phenomena; only this is the true characteristic of phenomena. It is not...
Those with false views may be compared [to this]. The profound purport of Prajñā reaches its ultimate subtlety here.

△ Doubt. Subhūti had already realized that the Dharma-body is the complete whole; he then doubted that the Dharma-body does not preach the Dharma, concluding that it is only the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) that preaches.
Furthermore, he held that the Dharma preached by the Transformation-body does not reach the realm of the Dharma-body.
Regarding the realms: how does one who upholds this Dharma obtain merit? It is because that which is taught by the nirmāṇakāya is itself the true Dharma, for the three bodies are of one essence.
Subhūti, if there were someone who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, were to offer them as a gift;

and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta and, taking up even as little as a four-line verse from this sūtra, were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others—their merit would surpass that of the former. How so? Because of explaining it to others.
He preached the Dharma without grasping at signs, remaining as such, unmoving.

This indicates that the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha preaches the Dharma of Suchness (tathatā). Subhūti raised a doubt, wondering how the Dharma preached by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha—which does not reach the realm of the Dharmakāya—could bring about merit. The Buddha said: "That which the Nirmāṇakāya preaches is itself the Dharma [of Suchness]."
It is taught through the body, for the three bodies are non-different. One who can uphold these four lines of this Dharma and expound them for others possesses the most supreme merit;
for they do not grasp at signs and remain unmoving within suchness. Reaching this state, one teaches in every dust mote, in every world-system, teaching with blazing intensity.
△ Doubt: The Dharma-body is quiescent; how can it be quiescent yet capable of preaching? Below, the correct contemplation is shown:

by means of the emptiness and quiescence of prajñā, one enters from the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) into emptiness. Because one enters emptiness from the provisional, it is called "true emptiness" (*bhūta-śūnyatā*); for the provisional is itself the true.
Why is this? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning.
One should contemplate them in this way.
This is the entry into the wondrous contemplation of the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of Prajñā. Because true emptiness is darkly quiescent, one contemplates it by means of the provisional.
If the contemplation through the six similes is perfected, then true emptiness will manifest of itself. These together reveal, from the outset, the essence of reality;
this is the correct demonstration of the method of contemplation, and all practitioners of the Way should enter by way of it. The true realm of the Dharma-body reaches its ultimate limit here.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās,
and all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
"Believing, accepting, and practicing.
This is the standard rule for concluding a sutra. Whenever one hears [the Dharma] with joy, it will surely accord perfectly with the mind.
When there is such accord, belief becomes genuine and acceptance becomes earnest; thus, the practice and observance will not be in vain.
The Diamond Resolve of Doubts (Concluded)
